title: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements (GAO-26-107859)
authors: US Government Accountability Office (contacts: William Russell; Candice N. Wright)
institution: US Government Accountability Office (GAO)
verification: GAO product page with highlights and recommendations read on gao.gov, 2026-11-05
relevance: GAO's dedicated audit of federal AI procurement: it reviewed 13 AI acquisitions at DOD, DHS, GSA and VA, finding that agencies more than doubled reported AI use from 2023 to 2024 and must navigate trade-offs between agency-directed vs vendor-driven acquisition, FAR-governed contracts vs other agreements, and AI-as-product vs AI-as-service. Key finding: agencies were not systematically collecting lessons learned (e.g., data-rights contract terms, testing requirements) and were unprepared to share them in GSA's repository because their policies did not require it. Four recommendations, all open, all concurred. Limitations: purposive sample of 13 acquisitions at 4 agencies, so not statistically representative. Attribution: the most direct federal watchdog evidence on how governments actually buy AI, complementing the CMU Block Center procurement guide already in the catalogue.

title: OMB Memorandum M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
authors: US Office of Management and Budget (Executive Office of the President)
institution: Office of Management and Budget, Executive Office of the President (United States)
verification: Summary page read on digitalgovernmenthub.org (issuance date April 3, 2025; requirements listed), 2026-11-05; original White House PDF blocked to automated fetching
relevance: The operative OMB memo governing US federal AI use, issued April 3, 2025 under Executive Order 14179: it directs agencies to expand AI adoption while preserving safeguards for civil rights, privacy and public accountability, requiring Chief AI Officers, AI governance boards, agency AI strategies, risk-tailored risk-management practices, public transparency and preference for American-made AI. It supersedes the March 2024 M-24-10, which had set mandatory minimum risk practices for 'rights-impacting' and 'safety-impacting' AI and is widely cited as the high-water mark of US government AI risk regulation — the pairing shows a deliberate pivot from risk-first to adoption-first governance. Limitations: the read summary page does not detail use-case reporting or the companion procurement memo (M-25-22), so those provisions need the primary text. Attribution: the central reference point for how the largest government AI user governs itself, and for procurement-relevant discretion over rights-impacting systems.

title: EU AI Model Contractual Clauses (MCC-AI) — Procurement of AI community, Public Buyers Community
authors: European Commission Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (DG GROW), with public buyers
institution: European Commission (Public Buyers Community)
verification: Community page read on public-buyers-community.ec.europa.eu, 2026-11-05 (clauses updated 5 March 2025; translations in all 24 EU languages announced 16 June 2025)
relevance: The EU's flagship practical instrument for procuring AI: model contractual clauses in full, light and guidance versions, designed to align public AI purchases with the AI Act and give administrations standard terms managing risks of AI solutions with 'checks and balances for their safe implementation'. Developed with the public-buyer community of practice and translated into all 24 EU languages by June 2025; the page also records follow-on demand signals such as the Irish Office of Government Procurement's AI market consultation (February 2026). Limitations: the clauses are voluntary templates, not binding law, and uptake across member states varies. Attribution: the concrete answer to 'what should an AI procurement contract actually say', complementing the JRC harmonised-standards brief already in the catalogue.

title: Draft National AI Development Strategy of Ukraine to 2030 (presented at the WINWIN Summit 2025)
authors: Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine (presented by Chief AI Officer Danilo Tsyvok and advisor Luukas Ilves)
institution: Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine
verification: Ministry's digitalstate.gov.ua news page read (translated from Ukrainian), 2026-11-05
relevance: Ukraine's successor to the 2020 AI Concept (Cabinet Order No. 1556-r): a draft strategy unveiled at the WINWIN Summit 2025 targeting a top-3 global position in AI development and public-sector integration, built on three priorities — practical AI impact across public services, defense, business, education and healthcare; sovereign and inclusive AI via national models; and infrastructure and talent. Its public-administration pillar is the wartime counterpart to Diia-style digital state building, with Estonia supporting the strategy's preparation through a development-cooperation project. Status: a draft opening for public consultation, feeding Ukraine's WINWIN Global Innovation Strategy to 2030. Limitations: unadopted draft, and war conditions make priorities and timelines volatile. Attribution: a rare documented case of AI governance strategy under existential pressure, from a jurisdiction the catalogue does not yet cover.

title: Bürokratt — Estonia's state AI virtual assistant for public services (Kratid programme)
authors: Estonian Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs; Information System Authority (RIA)
institution: Estonian Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs / Information System Authority (RIA)
verification: Official Bürokratt page read on kratid.ee including 2025-2026 roadmap milestones, 2026-11-05 (date field reflects the roadmap status documented on the page)
relevance: The operational instantiation of Estonia's KrattAI vision: a state-created, AI-based digital assistant network placed on public-sector websites so citizens can get information and use services conversationally, run by RIA under the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs. The page documents a real technology transition — early Rasa-based chatbots requiring manual training are shifting to LLM/RAG assistants drawing on institution-defined sources — with roadmap milestones: LLM+RAG deployment, a general knowledge module and a central 'global classifier' by end-2025, and personalized per-institution AI agents plus an Estonian-adapted LLM from 2026. Software is free, with roughly €150/month state-cloud hosting plus LLM usage fees, making it a reusable national pattern. Limitations: this is a program self-description with targets, not an independent evaluation of outcomes. Attribution: one of the most advanced operational government-assistant programmes anywhere, useful for discretion and street-level automation debates.

title: National Framework for the Assurance of Artificial Intelligence in Government
authors: Australian Government Data and Digital Ministers Meeting (published by the Department of Finance)
institution: Australian Government — Data and Digital Ministers Meeting (Commonwealth, state and territory governments)
verification: Framework page read on finance.gov.au, 2026-11-05 (agreed and released at the Data and Digital Ministers Meeting, 21 June 2024)
relevance: Australia's whole-of-government AI assurance instrument, agreed and released by the Data and Digital Ministers Meeting on 21 June 2024 by the Commonwealth and every state and territory government: it establishes cornerstones (five mechanisms) and practices of AI assurance that operationalise Australia's AI Ethics Principles in how governments assess AI they build and buy. The Digital Transformation Agency then ran a pilot (October 2024) testing a derived practical assurance framework with agencies. Limitations: it is a voluntary intergovernmental guideline rather than binding law, and assurance practice is still maturing through the pilot. Attribution: a distinctive federated model for government AI assurance — the same gap the ISO 42001 conformity-assessment ecosystem addresses commercially, but applied inside government.

title: Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems
authors: Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), Singapore
institution: Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), Singapore
verification: PDPC landing page read, 2026-11-05 (guidelines issued 1 March 2024; full PDF linked from the page)
relevance: Singapore's data-protection regulator explains when organisations may use personal data to develop and deploy AI recommendation and decision systems, walking through the AI lifecycle and clarifying consent/notification duties and PDPA exceptions (business improvement, research, legitimate interests) and data-minimisation expectations; law-firm analyses note the full document also touches the procurement stage of AI systems. Issued 1 March 2024, it applies to both private and public-sector adopters and complements Singapore's model AI governance framework already in the catalogue. Limitations: advisory rather than legally binding, and scoped to personal data rather than the full risk palette. Attribution: the clearest Southeast Asian articulation of how data-protection law binds AI deployment and procurement, from a jurisdiction frequently cited for pragmatic AI governance.

title: Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (New Zealand)
authors: New Zealand Government Digital Public Service (digital.govt.nz)
institution: New Zealand Government (Digital Public Service branch)
verification: Metadata only (lead): digital.govt.nz blocked automated fetching (Incapsula) on 2026-11-05; title, February 2025 version and its September 2023 interim predecessor confirmed via multiple web-search results only
relevance: New Zealand's public-service guidance on responsible generative AI use, published on digital.govt.nz in February 2025 as the successor to the September 2023 'Joint System Leads tactical guidance on Public Service use of GenAI' — a 13-page initial advisory from the data, digital, privacy, procurement and security system leaders. The 2025 guidance supports public servants to explore GenAI safely and transparently and sits alongside the broader Public Service AI Framework. Limitations: treated here as a lead record because the official page could not be fetched; content claims beyond title and lineage are not independently verified. Attribution: a small-state example of pragmatic, iteratively updated discretion guidance for civil servants using generative AI.

title: Algorithm Registers: A Box-Ticking Exercise or Meaningful Tool for Transparency?
authors: Esther Nieuwenhuizen (Utrecht University)
institution: Utrecht University (published in Information Polity, SAGE, Vol. 29 No. 4)
verification: Abstract, methods and full findings read on journals.sagepub.com, 2026-11-05 (published online 26 January 2025; issue dated November 2024)
relevance: The key empirical evaluation of the Amsterdam/Helsinki-style algorithm register model: 27 in-depth interviews with register developers and users (courts of audit, data protection authority, ombudsmen, journalists, NGOs) plus 33 policy documents in the Netherlands. Findings nuance both camps: public organisations selectively disclose (a form of 'openwashing'), registers are currently not useful to oversight authorities and societal watchdogs, and citizens barely use them — yet the registration process creates organisational awareness, learning and a 'disciplining effect' that pushes officials to justify legal basis and risks. The author concludes registers are 'not a meaningful tool for transparency, but a meaningful box-ticking exercise' and recommends targeting intermediaries and active oversight instead of citizens. Limitations: qualitative, Dutch-only, and a fast-moving field. Attribution: the definitive critical evidence base for the register-transparency strategy that Amsterdam, Helsinki and now the EU AI Act's registration duties rely on.

title: Algorithmes, systèmes d'IA et services publics : quels droits pour les usagers ? Points de vigilance et recommandations
authors: Défenseure des droits Claire Hédon (Défenseur des droits)
institution: Défenseur des droits (France's national ombudsman / rights defender institution)
verification: Official report page read on defenseurdesdroits.fr, 2026-11-05 (report dated 13 November 2024, 49 pages, PDFs in French and English linked)
relevance: France's principal rights-based official assessment of algorithmic government: the Défenseure des droits warns that the growing algorithmisation of public services endangers users' rights and sets out vigilance points on transparency, the right to know when an algorithm informed a decision, and the ability to contest it, with recommendations to make existing statutory guarantees fully effective. Published as French administrations scale up AI in citizen-facing services, it is the institutional counterweight to the state's own AI tooling (the official algorithm registry and sovereign AI assistants). Limitations: the web page gives only a short summary — the detailed vigilance points and recommendations sit in the PDF; recommendations are non-binding on the administration. Attribution: the reference document on users' rights versus automated public administration in France, and a template for ombudsman-style AI oversight elsewhere.

title: Amendments to the Directive on Automated Decision-Making (following the third review) — Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat
authors: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat (Office of the Chief Human Resources Officer / Chief Information Officer of Canada)
institution: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat (Government of Canada)
verification: canada.ca amendments announcement read, 2026-11-05 (amendments effective 25 April 2023; new systems compliant by 25 October 2023, existing systems by 25 April 2024); third-review process details cross-checked on the GCcollab Third Review page
relevance: The amendment package resulting from the third review of Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making — the world's first national algorithmic-impact-assessment regime (in force since April 2020): scope extended to internal services (hiring, performance management, security screening), Algorithmic Impact Assessments and peer-review findings must now be published before a system launches, the review cycle moved to two years, and requirements were strengthened for bias testing, data governance, explanation, GBA+ and impacts on persons with disabilities. The review itself found gaps in transparency, accountability and fairness, plus feasibility and terminology problems. Limitations: the AIA tool is frequently criticised as paperwork-heavy, and self-assessment scores have been questioned for consistency. Attribution: the most-tracked national model of mandatory pre-deployment AI impact assessment and disclosure, and the reference case when evaluating the EU AI Act's similar registry logic.

title: Report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
authors: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Commissioner: The Hon Catherine Holmes AC SC)
institution: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Commonwealth of Australia)
verification: Commission's publications page read including the full list of 57 recommendations and chapters on automated decision-making, 2026-11-05
relevance: The final report (three volumes, presented to the Governor-General on 7 July 2023) of the inquiry into Australia's automated income-compliance 'robodebt' scheme, which raised unlawful welfare debts from income averaging; the Commission found the scheme was unlawful, 'crude and cruel', and that institutions failed to heed warnings from staff, lawyers and the Ombudsman. Its Chapter 17 recommendations on automated decision-making remain a template: legislative reform to create a consistent legal framework for automation in government services, plain-language public information, availability of business rules and algorithms for independent expert scrutiny, and a standing body to monitor and audit automated decision-making. 57 recommendations in total, with referrals concerning individual officials. Limitations: retrospective; implementation depends on the government response. Attribution: the most consequential official accountability document on algorithmic harm to welfare recipients anywhere, and a standard citation in debates on automated decision-making and administrative law.

title: NJCM, CILP, Foss and Joosse v the Netherlands (SyRI judgment), Rechtbank Den Haag, ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:1878
authors: District Court of The Hague (counsel: NJCM, CILP, Foss research centre, SyRI victim Jose; judgment in case C-09-550982)
institution: District Court of The Hague (Rechtbank Den Haag), the Netherlands
verification: Metadata only (lead): rechtspraak.nl judgment and press-release pages blocked automated fetching on 2026-11-05; the holding (Wet SyRI violates Article 8 ECHR; use to cease) corroborated from the court's official press-release headline, the Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor summary and academic case notes (van Bekkum 2021; Rachovitsa & Trompeter 2022) surfaced in web search
relevance: The first ruling worldwide to strike down a government welfare-fraud risk-profiling algorithm on human-rights grounds: on 5 February 2020 the District Court of The Hague held that the SyRI legislation (Welfare and Work Inspection Reuse Act) violated Article 8 ECHR because the interference was not 'in accordance with the law' — the risk model was insufficiently transparent, safeguards against arbitrary use were lacking, and the fair balance tipped against residents of low-income neighbourhoods; SyRI use was ordered to cease immediately. Limitations: the judgment predates the 2023-2026 window (kept because it is the canonical in-court document for this requested case), and its technical reasoning covers a rule-based system rather than machine learning. Attribution: the foundational precedent for algorithmic accountability litigation, cited across EU AI Act debates and welfare-automation cases.

title: Ongekend onrecht — Final report of the Parliamentary Interrogation Committee on the childcare benefits scandal (POK)
authors: Parlementaire ondervragingscommissie kinderopvangtoeslag (chaired by Chris van Dam; vice-chair Attje Kuiken)
institution: House of Representatives of the Netherlands (Tweede Kamer)
verification: Tweede Kamer POK committee page read, 2026-11-05 (report presented 17 December 2020; eight days of hearings in November 2020, 19 people interrogated including Prime Minister Rutte; report PDF linked from the page)
relevance: The Dutch Parliament's own interrogation of the toeslagenaffaire: the POK report 'Ongekend onrecht' documents how the Tax Administration's wrongfully designed fraud risk model (the dual-nationality classifier) and the harshly enforced Fraud Signalling Facility (FSV) drove tens of thousands of families into debt and hardship, while ministers ignored warnings — culminating in the Cabinet's resignation on 15 January 2021. Eight days of public hearings examined nineteen serving and former officials and ministers. Limitations: the December 2020 report predates the 2023-2026 window (kept as the canonical official document for this requested case), and the page itself documents process rather than findings, which live in the PDF; a follow-on parliamentary inquiry into fraud policy and service delivery is examining institutional lessons. Attribution: the pivotal documented case linking algorithmic risk profiling, administrative discretion and democratic accountability, and the direct catalyst for the Dutch algorithm register and EU-level algorithm rules.

title: ISO/IEC 42006:2025 — Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Requirements for bodies providing audit and certification of AI management systems
authors: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 (joint technical committee)
institution: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 (ISO and IEC)
verification: ISO catalogue page read on iso.org, 2026-11-05 (Edition 1, published 7 July 2025, 31 pages; CHF 159, preview on the ISO Online Browsing Platform)
relevance: The conformity-assessment layer of the ISO 42001 ecosystem: ISO/IEC 42006:2025 specifies requirements for certification bodies that audit and certify AI management systems, supplementing ISO/IEC 17021-1 with AI-specific auditor competence and process requirements so that third-party AIMS certification is consistent and credible; it can also be folded into product/service certification schemes under ISO/IEC 17065. This is the operational answer to 'who audits the auditors' as ISO/IEC 42001 certificates proliferate under the EU AI Act's conformity-assessment logic. Limitations: paywalled, and the certification market it governs is young — the value of an AIMS certificate against actual AI risk is still untested. Attribution: the missing piece that turns ISO/IEC 42001 from a management-system template into an auditable assurance regime, distinct from the ISO 42001 standard itself already in the catalogue.

title: CEN and CENELEC adopt exceptional measures to accelerate AI standardization for the EU AI Act (JTC 21, M/593 and M/613)
authors: CEN and CENELEC (joint Technical Boards; CEN-CLC/JTC 21 'Artificial Intelligence')
institution: CEN-CENELEC (European Committee for Standardization / European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardization)
verification: CEN-CENELEC news page read, 2026-11-05 (Technical Boards meeting of 14-16 October 2025; announcement published 23 October 2025)
relevance: The clearest official status report on the EU AI Act's harmonised-standards bottleneck: to speed up JTC 21 deliverables requested under standardisation mandates M/593 and M/613, CEN and CENELEC adopted exceptional measures — skipping the formal vote where the Enquiry vote is positive (a legitimate procedure under Internal Regulations Part 2, Article 11.2) and creating a small drafting group of active experts to finalise the six most delayed drafts. Standards are now targeted for availability by Q4 2026, with Enquiry launching for prEN 18286 (quality management systems), a key deliverable for the future AI Act conformity-assessment framework. Limitations: this is an exceptional, temporary measure and the timeline has already slipped repeatedly (from late 2025 toward end-2026), which pressures the AI Act's high-risk obligations. Attribution: primary evidence of how far the EU's standards-based AI governance actually is from finished, complementing the JRC brief already in the catalogue.

title: The NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Adoption Challenges and Opportunities
authors: Gillian Kennedy, Devin Patel, Humza Sheikh, Paul Wagner, Robert J. Honomichl (University of Arizona)
institution: University of Arizona (published in Journal of Cybersecurity Education, Research and Practice, Kennesaw State University Digital Commons, Vol. 2026, No. 1)
verification: Article landing page with abstract read on digitalcommons.kennesaw.edu, 2026-11-05
relevance: A peer-reviewed, implementation-focused evaluation of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework: the paper situates the Govern-Map-Measure-Manage functions against the EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001 as complementary frameworks and concludes that 'the primary obstacle to effective AI governance is not a lack of standards but inconsistent and incomplete organizational implementation'. It documents adoption barriers specific to small and medium-sized enterprises and proposes improvements across organisations of different size and maturity. Limitations: a US business/cybersecurity lens rather than a public-sector one, and this record was verified at abstract level rather than full text. Attribution: a direct published critique of the framework that US agencies and firms most use to operationalise AI risk management — the evaluation layer the catalogue lacked alongside NIST AI RMF 1.0 itself.

title: Pour une intelligence artificielle au service de l'intérêt général — CESE opinion (with citizen participation)
authors: Conseil économique, social et environnemental (CESE), temporary AI commission with 10 citizens selected by lot
institution: Conseil économique, social et environnemental (CESE), France
verification: Metadata only (lead): lecese.fr blocked automated fetching on 2026-11-05; opinion verified via detailed ActuIA coverage of the adopted text (adoption by 99 votes to 22 abstentions and 10 against on 14 January 2025; 224-page PDF and group statements listed on the official page surfaced in search)
relevance: France's third constitutional assembly delivered the civil-society contribution to the Paris AI Action Summit: an opinion drafted by a CESE commission of organised civil society members alongside ten citizens selected by lot, adopted in plenary on 14 January 2025. It proposes an acceptability framework with four inseparable criteria — planetary boundaries, social progress, economic issues and fundamental rights — and 32 recommendations including a national interprofessional agreement on AI at work, mass AI training (citing 16 million French people distant from digital tools), a human option in public services, and transparency about AI's energy and water footprint. Limitations: advisory to government and parliament rather than binding; treated as a lead record because the official page could not be fetched directly. Attribution: a rare institutionalised model of citizen participation inside a constitutional body's AI policy output.

title: Building Resilient Democracies by Putting Citizens at the Heart of Policymaking: Exploring New Frontiers in Citizen Participation in the Policy Cycle
authors: OECD (Public Governance Directorate)
institution: OECD
verification: Metadata only (lead): OECD.org report pages fetched 2026-11-05 returned site navigation with the report body truncated; title, March 2025 publication and deliberative-wave/database framing confirmed via OECD publication listings and the OECD Reinforcing Democracy Initiative (October 2024) in web search
relevance: The OECD's update on the 'deliberative wave' and the next frontiers of citizen participation, drawing on the OECD deliberative democracy database: the 2024 database update collected 160 new representative deliberative processes, extending coverage to 34 countries (about 96% of documented cases sit in OECD member countries — a skew the OECD itself flags), and the report extends the deliberative-wave framework to newer formats, including deliberation about artificial intelligence and AI-enabled participation. Limitations: treated as a lead record because OECD web pages would not render their body content to automated fetching, so specific chapter findings are not independently verified here. Attribution: the reference quantitative data source on institutionalised citizen participation worldwide, the evidence base behind citizens' assemblies as a governance instrument.

title: How we govern AI — Barcelona's municipal AI governance model and public algorithm registry
authors: Ajuntament de Barcelona (Barcelona Innovation and Technology / Municipal Institute for Innovation and Technology)
institution: Ajuntament de Barcelona (Barcelona City Council)
verification: Official city page read, 2026-11-05 (page undated; an associated file upload suggests July 2026 currency, so the date field reflects page status as accessed)
relevance: Barcelona's self-description of its municipal AI governance model, built on 'technological humanism': an Executive Committee steering the Strategy for the Ethical, Democratic and Sustainable Adoption of AI; an AI Office within BIT coordinating and monitoring municipal AI projects; an independent Advisory Council on AI, Ethics and Digital Rights that evaluates high-risk systems and publishes its reports; continuous risk assessment aligned with the EU AI Act; and a public algorithm registry hosted on the city's transparency portal — which the city says made it a pioneer in Spain, following the Amsterdam/Helsinki register precedents. Participatory elements run through collaboration with universities, research centres and social organisations. Limitations: an official self-description with no independent evaluation, and the page is undated. Attribution: the leading Southern-European city-level model combining a municipal algorithm register with an independent ethics review body.

title: Null Compliance: NYC Local Law 144 and the Challenges of Algorithm Accountability
authors: Lucas Wright, Roxana Mike Muenster, Briana Vecchione, et al. (with Jacob Metcalf and J. Nathan Matias; 155 student investigators)
institution: Cornell University with Data & Society (published in Proceedings of the 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, FAccT '24)
verification: Abstract and methods read on arxiv.org, 2026-11-05 (ACM FAccT 2024 proceedings DOI 10.1145/3630106.3658998)
relevance: The definitive empirical study of the first bias-audit mandate for commercial algorithmic hiring systems: in Local Law 144's first year, 155 student investigators examined 391 employers and found only 18 posted the required bias audit reports and just 13 posted transparency notices. The paper's core concept, 'null compliance', shows that because employers have discretion over whether their tool falls within the law's scope, an absent audit cannot be treated as non-compliance — and nearly all audits that were posted reported impact factors above 0.8, a threshold borrowed from employment-discrimination caselaw. Conclusions: discretion granted to regulated parties and reliance on transparency and end-user accountability are structural weaknesses of audit mandates. Limitations: one jurisdiction, first-year snapshot; the New York State Comptroller's December 2025 audit later documented enforcement gaps at DCWP. Attribution: the evidence base for what actually happens when a city mandates algorithmic audits — the reality check for the NYC AEDT page already in the catalogue.

title: Algorithmic transparency recording standard: guidance for public sector organisations (ATRS)
authors: UK Government Digital Service (GDS) / Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO)
institution: UK Government Digital Service (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology)
verification: gov.uk guidance page read, 2026-11-05 (first published 5 January 2023, updated 8 May 2025; mandatory scope policy linked from the page)
relevance: The UK's schema-based standard for publishing records of algorithmic tools used in the public sector on GOV.UK: the ATRS gives public bodies a fixed template (owner, decision type, data, human oversight) so citizens and oversight bodies can see how government uses algorithms. It is already mandatory for central government organisations, with voluntary uptake by the wider public sector, and GDS announced in May 2025 plans to complete publication of records and extend the mandate across government. Limitations: records are self-reported, coverage is uneven, and there is little active compliance verification — the same limitations Nieuwenhuizen's Dutch register study documents. Attribution: the most mature national implementation of a government AI use register, and the model the OECD has promoted internationally — the concrete answer to catalogue item (g) on government AI use reporting.
